full_judgment:
Under challenge in this Rule is the judgment and order dated 17-7-94 passed by the District Judge, Lakshmipur in Misc. Appeal No. 2 of 1993 reversing those dated 29-11-92 by the learned Assistant Judge, Ramgonj in Misc. Case No. 1 of 1992 allowing the Misc. Case under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. 

 5. Opposite Party Nos. 1 and 2 contested the suit by filing a joint written objection contending, inter alia, that there is no cause of action; that the case is barred by limitation, estoppel and defect of parties. It was further stated that the deed in question was an exchange deed and not a sale. The ''Ka'' schedule land which is a pond and to the east of the said pond the opposite party No. 1 had built a new house and hence he needed the ''ka'' schedule property more so because that property was not that much useful to the opposite party No. 2. The ''Kha'' schedule land being situated by the side of a canal is useful for business and, as such, is a valuable property. The opposite party No. 2 was in need of the said property. Accordingly, the opposite party No. 1 exchanged his ''Kha'' schedule property with that of the ''Ka'' schedule property of opposite party No. 2 and in that way the opposite party No. 1 became the owner in possession of ''Ka'' schedule property and opposite party No. 2 became owner in possession of ''Kha'' schedule property. Their further case is that the value of the suit property is Taka 10,000.00 and for the purpose of exchange the value was shown as Taka 3,000.00. 

 10. Mr. Md Ozair Farooq, learned Advocate appearing for the petitioners, strongly supported the judgment and order passed by the Assistant Judge, Ramgonj and very virulently assailed those of the appellate Court. Mr. Farooq submits: a) that the District Judge erred in holding that the disputed deed is a "deed of exchange" and nota deed of sale b) that the District Judge also erred in holding that the PWs indirectly or by implication admitted that opposite party Nos. 1 and 2 in between them had an exchange in respect of ''Ka'' and ''Kha'' schedule land by using, the expression “জেরার জবাবে পরোক্ষভাবে হইলেও স্বীকার করিয়াছে যে ১/২ নং প্রতিপক্ষ আপীলগন নং ‘ক’ তপছিল বর্ণিত ভূমি এওয়াজ বিনিময় করিয়াছে।   inasmuch as no such indirect admission can be inferred from the cross-examination of the PWs on record. In order to put emphasis and find out the fallacy that an error has been committed by the court of appeal below he has referred to the deposition of PWs Haran Chandra Sil who stated that opposite party Nos. 1 and 2 and the land in schedule ''Ka'' and ''Kha'' respectively are known to him and he came to know from different sources that opposite party No. 2 Sree Partha Banik sold out the ''Ka’ schedule land to opposite party No. 1 Md. Mosharraf Hossain. Mr Farooq also referred to the deposition of PW 4 Md Hanif who also corroborated PW 2 Haran Chandra Sil by stating that he heard before that Sree Partha Banik sold out the disputed property to Md Mosharraf Hossain, then said that they made an ewaj and used the expression —“আগে শুনিয়াছে খরিদ বিক্রয় করে পরে শুনিয়াছি এওয়াজ বদল হইয়াছে। c) Mr Farooq also submits that the court of appeal below committed an error of law by ignoring the contradiction in the deposition of OPWs 1 and 2 in respect of possession of ''Kha'' schedule land by opposite party No. 1 Sree Partha Banik and without adverting to the finding of facts as regards lack of delivery of possession of ''kha'' schedule land to the opposite party No. 2 pursuant to the alleged exchange the court of appeal below reversed the decision of the trial Court and in so doing MrFarooq referred to the deposition of DW 2 Sree Partha Banik who in his cross-examination stated that “জমি না মাপিয়া দখল দিয়াছিল” although from schedule ''Kha'' it is clear that the quantum of land in that schedule is 2.92 acres and out of that only a small fraction of 2-1/2 acres was exchanged. Mr Farooq also referred to the deposition of PW 1 namely, opposite party No. 1 Md. Mosharraf Hossain who stated that the ''Kha'' schedule land which is to the west of his house is a high land situated by the side of Khal and that the distance between la'' and Kha'' schedule land is one mile and the two schedules form part of 2 (two) different Pourashavas. He further stated that his residence is in Mouza Nandanpur but he could not recollect the plot number and the Khatian of his house and he could not file any paper and document in support of his contention that the said house belonged to him; that the ''Kha'' schedule land is adjacent to his house and the same is high land (vhiti) by the side of a canal and the said fact is also corroborated by DW 2 Partha Banik stating “খ” তপছিল ভূমি খাল সংলগ্ন ভিটি জমি”। 

 11. But in his cross examination PW 2 categorically stated that he got the ''Kha'' schedule land cultivated through Abut Kashem and received 5 maunds of paddy. He failed to name the person who planted the seedlings in the land. PW2 also stated that by engaging 4 labourers for the whole day he harvested the paddy grown on 2-1/2 decimals of land. It is not understood as to how a small fraction of 2-1/2 decimals of land, admittedly bhiti land, could yield 5 maunds of paddy. PW2 in his cross examination also stated that he himself as well as PW 1 Md Mosharraf Hossain are owners of contiguous shop, and that the ''Ka'' schedule land is at a distance of one mile from his house and Kazirkhil is about 3 miles away from his house. On a reference to PW 2 Md Fazlul Hoque it appears that OPW 1 Md Mosharraf Hossain got a portion of the pond and OPW 2 Partha Banik got bhiti land. On a reference to PW 1 Mosharraf Hossain it is also seen that the possession of ''Ka'' schedule land was delivered on the 7th of Agrahyan at about 11-00 AM and on the following day i.e. on the 8th of Agrahyan schedule ''Kha'' land was delivered to Partha Banik at about 11/12 AM. 

 (5) At the first hearing of the suit the Court shall, after reading the plaint and the written statements, if any, and after such examination of the parties as may appear necessary, ascertain upon what material propositions of fact or of law the parties are at variance, and shall thereupon proceed to frame and record the issues on which the right decision of the case appears to depend. 

 14. If proper issues are not framed, it is an irregularity which may or may not be a material one. If such omission has affected the disposal of the case on the merits it will be a ground for remanding the case for a new trial. But if, on the other hand, parties have not been prejudiced by the omission and substantial justice has been done in the case, notwithstanding the omission to frame issues, the decision will not be set aside or case remanded for a new trial and this view of mine finds support in a case reported in PLD 1969 Pesh 241 and PLD 1969 Pesh. 5. If, though no issue is framed on the fact, the parties adduce evidence on the fact and discuss it before the Court, and. the Court decides the point, as if there was an issue framed on it, the decision will not be set aside in appeal on the ground merely that no issue was framed. Certain allegations made in the plaint were challenged in the written statement, but issues were not framed Held that the Court was competent to allow the parties to lead evidence on such points. The reason is that mere omission to frame an issue is not fatal to the trial of a suit. Omission to frame an issue is an irregularity which may or may not affect the disposal of a suit on the merits. If it does, the appellate Court should remand the case for a new trial to the lower Court after framing the necessary issue. If it does not, the appellate Court should not remand the case. In the instant case the court of appeal below though found fault with the trial Court for not framing any issue, did not send the case back on remand by framing proper issues, rather reversed the judgment and order of the trial Court in spite of the fact that all the points on which the parties did not agree were duly considered and decision arrived at. In the case of Mitna vs. Syed Fazl their Lordships of the Privy Council said: 

 15. In view of the facts, circumstances, as well as the evidence on record and for the foregoing reasons I am inclined to hold that the learned Assistant Judge, Ramgonj was absolutely correct in allowing the pre-emption holding that the deed of sale being described as an ewaj cannot stand in the way of the exercise of the right of pre-emption allowed under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act and the court of appeal committed an error of law resulting in an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice in not affirming the judgment of the trial Court in spite of the fact that substantial justice was done by the trial Court and in that view of the matter the impugned judgment and order do call for interference by this court.
